newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek PM will push quiet diplomacy after win.
newsitem.headline: Greek PM will push quiet diplomacy after win.

text.p: Greek socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis's election win gives him a free hand to pick his cabinet and forge the "new era" policies which he says are essential to modernise the EU's only Balkan state.

Simitis, 60, is the first fresh face at the helm of Greece in 20 years and he is determined to make the country fit in with the rest of the European Union after years of being mocked and branded the odd man out, diplomats said.

"He is adamant Greece must move forward with a dramatically different approach to economic and foreign policy. He is personally offended that Greece is at the bottom of almost every EU list," said an EU diplomat.
Often billed as a competent technocrat, trained in economics and commercial law, he has shown during a meteoric rise to power over the past eight months that he can be tough.

He sailed masterfully from replacing ailing socialist party founder Andreas Papandreou as premier in January, to capturing the party leadership in June and capped it all with a solid win in his first national campaign.
"Everyone has learned that Simitis doesn't play around. If he wants someone out, if they don't fit in with his plans, he will remove them," a socialist official said.
The first test will come this week when Simitis names his cabinet. Top ministers -- defence, national economy and foreign affairs -- are expected to change as he shapes his team.

Simitis was educated in Germany and Britain and he is deeply committed to the EU. Diplomats said it was already clear that he viewed the world through EU eyes instead of the distorting prism of the Balkans.
His priority will be improving Greece's image by meeting EU economic convergence targets. He is expected to apply stringent economic measures and more belt-tightening for the Greek public.
"He will push for faster modernisation and convergence with the EU, which is the heart of his philosophy," said Costas Avranitopoulos of the Institute for International Relations.
"Austerity will continue but there will be a development element in his policy," he said.

Greece's ponderous public sector is choked with red tape and slowed by sleepy officials. Privatisation programmes have crept forward and poor adminstration has meant an excruciatingly slow pace of spending EU funds earmarked for public works projects.
Simitis is expected to look for tough, competent ministers who can shake things up and are not afraid of taking on strong special interest groups in forcing through modernisation.

"He will try to put things in order but his austerity plan needs the compliance of the trade unions. That may prove to be his biggest headache," Thanos Veremis, director of the Hellenic Foundation for European and Foreign Policy, said.
Diplomats said Simitis sees economic renewal and better EU relations as the only realistic approach to containing Greece's recurring nightmare -- neighbouring Turkey.
He will turn to the International Court, and lobby EU states and Washington to pressure Turkey in various regional disputes. His approach will be more active but not confrontational.
Diplomats said his big challenge will be Turkey, with whom tensions have risen dramatically this year and the feuding NATO allies almost going to war over an uninhabited Aegean island.
"The danger comes when he realises there is very little the EU or international organisations can do to make Turkey behave as Athens might wish," another EU diplomat said.
"He might then seen the only option as a strong military, which is expensive and difficult to combine with the cost of domestic development and drowth," he added.
One of Simitis's first decisions is likely to be dropping Defence Minister Gerassimos Arsenis, a Papandreou holdover who wants to spend $10 billion on a major new arms build-up.
